implementation_notes: The Kotlin standard library ships the pattern as DeepRecursiveFunction<T, R>: its documentation states that it keeps the recursion's stack on the heap so very deep computations do not use the actual call stack, that callRecursive performs the logical call, and that other DeepRecursiveFunction instances can be called through callRecursive in the same scope - which is what makes mutual recursion safe; the same page recommends it once recursion goes deeper than about a thousand calls. The tailrec modifier is not a substitute: the compiler only turns a function into a loop when the function is self-recursive and the call is the final operation, so mutually recursive functions still overflow with it. Hand-roll a step type only when the stdlib cannot be used or the steps must be interleaved with a custom scheduler.
pitfalls: The heap stack means deep or diverging recursion consumes memory instead of the VM stack, so a runaway recursion now surfaces as memory pressure or GC time.
tailrec looks like the same tool but silently does nothing for mutual recursion; the compiler only warns when the formal conditions are unmet, so verify with a deep input.
Because the recursion no longer appears in stack traces, failures must be diagnosed by instrumenting the lambda body or by counting callRecursive invocations.
